articles.title: Palestinians bury remains of 105 people killed in Israeli attack on Gaza
articles.summary: Family members of the victims performed funeral prayers over the remains, which were wrapped in Palestinian flags.
articles.body:
Hundreds of people attended a mass funeral for 105 Palestinians killed in a devastating Israeli attack on Gaza City in October 2023.

Family members of the victims performed funeral prayers over the remains, which were wrapped in Palestinian flags, before they were taken to Martyrs Cemetery in the Sheikh Radwan neighborhood, northwest of Gaza City, and buried, Palestinian news agency Wafa reported on Thursday.

The victims were killed in a series of Israeli air strikes involving at least 20 bombs that levelled the seven-storey Al Taj 3 building and destroyed several other residential buildings in the Yarmouk Square neighbourhood on the afternoon of October 25, 2023, as part of Israel’s ongoing genocidal war .

According to Al Jazeera’s Hani Mahmoud, many of those killed were displaced families “who were staying with their relatives after they were forced to flee … the horror of the carpet bombing of the northern part of the Strip”.

He described the mood ahead of the funeral early on Thursday as one filled with “grief” but also said the ceremony provided “long-awaited closure”.

“After nearly three years of uncertainty … those who survived, their relatives … they’re going to say goodbye.”

Gaza’s civil defence said the recovery operation was carried out in coordination with an Egyptian committee.

Al Jazeera correspondent Ibrahim al-Khalili, reporting from Gaza City, said the operation was the fifth-largest of its kind since Israel launched its genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza in October 2023, in terms of the number of bodies recovered.

Civil defence operations director Abdul al-Majdalawi said it had been “impossible” to reach the bodies at the time of the attack.

“Bulldozers, excavators and other heavy machinery used by civil defence teams in Gaza were directly and deliberately targeted,” he said.

Osama Sharaf said 37 members of his family were killed in the attack.

“We recovered some of them at the beginning of the war, and today [Wednesday], 16 more were recovered, including my father, my mother and all of my siblings. My sister’s son was also there with them,” he said.

Despite the so-called “ceasefire” agreed upon last October, Israeli attacks on Gaza have continued, with eight Palestinians killed in the last 24 hours, including a child, a woman and a journalist.

At least 1,431 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since the “truce” took effect, according to Palestinian health authorities.

“Since the ceasefire was signed back in October 2025, nearly a year now, we’re looking at more than 5,000 violations by the Israeli military,” said Mahmoud.

“People are very worried now just to step outside in the streets … what’s supposed to be normal days are not.”

According to Sultan Barakat, a professor of public policy at Qatar Foundation’s Hamad Bin Khalifa University, the international community has been unable to hold Israel accountable and has not been able to restrain Israel from “having a free hand in Gaza”.

“There were a number of issues that the Israelis should have done in order to progress the agreement,” Barakat told Al Jazeera.

Israelis continued to talk about the total disarmament of Hamas, even while no international force has been brought in to provide security, as was stated in the original agreement, he said.

“There is no one to protect the Palestinians. There’s no one to ensure security on the streets in Gaza,” said Barakat.

articles.title: Parra: "Radio Marca siempre ha salido a ganar"
articles.standfirst: Pablo Parra, presentador de 'Marcador', segundo invitado de 'Frecuencia Marca'
articles.summary: Pablo Parra, presentador de 'Marcador', segundo invitado de 'Frecuencia Marca'
articles.body: Pablo Parra, ahora al frente de 'Marcador', visita 'Frecuencia Marca' para charlar sobre sus orígenes, su amor por el periodismo y sus objetivos con Radio Marca... que apuntan a lo más alto. PREGUNTA: ¿Cómo empezó en esto del periodismo? RESPUESTA: Creo que yo solo sé ser periodista, desde que soy pequeño siempre lo he querido ser. Cuando vi que el fútbol no iba a ser lo mío, porque era una cuestión bastante evidente, empecé a ver que a mí me gustaba contar el fútbol. P: ¿Entonces ha cumplido el sueño que tenía desde niño? R: Creo que los he cumplido todos, por suerte. Aquí en Radio Marca me han dado la oportunidad de estar en un Mundial, he contado un Mundial femenino y hace poquito se ha cumplido el otro sueño que yo tenía, porque yo era uno de los que los domingos a las cinco de la tarde ponía Carrusel Deportivo con Paco, con Manolo, con Pepe Domingo y con toda esta gente. Ahora pienso que habrá niños que se van a poner 'mi Marcador' y estarán al otro lado de la radio como me ponía yo de pequeño. P: Y si nos remontamos a sus inicios en la profesión, ¿qué es lo que recuerda de una forma más especial? R: Recuerdo que el primer día que yo llegué a la Universidad Complutense hay una radio que se llama Inforadio y pregunté: "Oye, ¿qué hay que hacer aquí para hacer radio?". El primer día ya nos pusieron a un grupo de chavales y a mí en un programa que se llamaba La Otra Mañana y ahí empecé. P: ¿Y en Radio Marca? R: El primer día que tuve que venir aquí a la redacción fue un lunes. Me acuerdo que tenía que entrar a las siete de la tarde porque mi turno era nocturno. Estaba súper nervioso. Además, me acuerdo que me salió hasta un grano del fin de semana de los nervios que tenía. Ese primer día de la redacción fue poner cara a la gente que yo escuchaba porque yo era un oyente más de Radio Marca. Recuerdo que luego me vino a buscar mi madre. No sé, la verdad que tengo un recuerdo muy bonito de ese primer día. P: ¿Y cómo recuerda esa transición de estar estudiando y de estar en Inforadio a llegar a Radio Marca? R: Hice prácticas en un sitio que se llamaba 'Fichajes.com', donde aprendí mucho, pero yo sabía que quería estar en la radio. Me puse a buscar pero no encontraba nada, hasta que un día un compañero mío que estaba aquí de prácticas, en Marca, me dijo: "Si es que tú solo quieres Radio Marca" y le dije: "Es cierto". Un día me llamó Miguel Gómez, un jueves, cogí el teléfono y me convocaron para ir al día siguiente a firmar para empezar el lunes, porque había habido una baja de un chaval de Murcia, que le estaré eternamente agradecido. Así surgió. P: De esas primeras veces en Radio Marca, ¿hay algún momento que tenga marcado de forma especial? R: Los Juegos Olímpicos de Río de 2016 para mí son muy especiales porque yo creo que es lo que, como redactor de la radio, me sitúan un poco entre esa hornada buena de becarios que teníamos. Y claro, los Juegos Olímpicos los hicimos José Rodríguez, que por aquel entonces era colaborador, y la ceremonia de apertura de esos Juegos Olímpicos la hacemos José Rodríguez y dos becarios. Ahora lo pienso y siento el privilegio que fue porque yo es que no llevaba en la radio ni tres meses. P: ¿Qué importancia ha tenido en su carrera el fútbol femenino? R: Brutal. Yo siempre digo que yo no quiero sacar pecho porque yo no aposté por el fútbol femenino. A mí el fútbol femenino me llegó. Son cosas de la vida que no piensas que van a ser tan importantes en tu carrera, pero ahí se quedó y me ha dado, de entrada, experiencias de vida que son brutales. Mis mejores viajes han sido con el fútbol femenino. P: Y cuéntame, ¿cómo llega usted a Marcador? R: Recuerdo llegar a casa cansado de trabajar durante este Mundial y López me dice que se va a ir a Radio Nacional. La mañana siguiente hablamos Amaro y yo y me dice que si quiero dar ese paso, que lo piense. Entonces yo hablo con mi pareja, que le estaré agradecido eternamente, porque es difícil el decir quiero estar con un periodista deportivo y más que vaya a trabajar los fines de semana... Pero lo pensé y acepté. P: ¿Y qué podemos esperar de Marcador y de Pablo Parra en el futuro? R: De mí lo que se puede esperar es lo que siempre he sentido, creo que más que yo no va a trabajar nadie. En Marcador, el protagonista es el balón, el narrador. Tú tienes que asumir un papel de estar pendiente de todas las canchas. Radio Marca y Marca siempre han salido a ganar y nosotros salimos también a competir con todo, al máximo nivel que podamos dar. ¿Su olor favorito? La paella. ¿El insulto que más usa? Cabrón. ¿Y la mentira? He dicho durante mucho tiempo "estoy bien" cuando no lo estaba, pero ya he decidido no mentir más en eso. ¿Qué es lo que más vergüenza ajena le da? Cuando un periodista defiende en su equipo lo que le critica en otro. ¿Un miedo absurdo? Me da mucho miedo tener una enfermedad que me prive de poder vivir los años que viva bien. ¿El contacto más famoso de su agenda? Que me responda, Vicente del Bosque, pero tengo, por ejemplo, el contacto del Cholo.

articles.title: Ex-fraternity leader at Arizona university gets jail time after pledge died of alcohol poisoning
articles.summary: A former Northern Arizona University fraternity leader was sentenced to two months in jail for his role in a hazing that led to the death of a pledge student.
articles.body: FLAGSTAFF, Ariz. — A former Northern Arizona University fraternity leader was sentenced to two months in jail Wednesday for his role in a hazing that led to the death of a pledge student. Carter Eslick, 20, also received three years of supervised probation during a sentencing hearing in Coconino County Superior Court. Eslick had pleaded guilty to a felony hazing charge in the Jan. 31 death of Colin Daniel Martinez, 18, at an off-campus house. An autopsy found Martinez died of alcohol poisoning with a blood-alcohol content of 0.425% — more than five times the state’s legal limit for drivers 21 and over. Martinez was among four Delta Tau Delta pledges who shared two bottles of vodka to ensure they vomited, according to court documents. Witnesses reported adjusting Martinez’s sleeping position and checking his pulse and breathing to look for signs of alcohol poisoning throughout the night, the documents said. Martinez’s parents appeared remotely in court, still grieving their son, and said they want accountability and reform within Greek life, Phoenix television station azfamily.com reported. Eslick was the fraternity’s pledge master at the time and was responsible for welcoming new members. He apologized Wednesday to Martinez’s family and said he takes “full responsibility for the hand I played in that ritual.” Coconino County Attorney Ammon Barker said no sentence can undo the harm to the Martinez family. “My hope is that this case helps people understand the serious dangers of hazing and encourages them to speak up and intervene before another family experiences this kind of loss,” Barker said in a statement. Judge Stacy Krueger said Eslick knew what he did was dangerous and was troubled that no one spoke out against it. Eslick could face additional jail time if he doesn’t meet the conditions of probation, which include creating and delivering 305 anti-hazing presentations and keeping the court updated on his progress. He also can’t use alcohol or drugs unless prescribed. The university suspended the fraternity after Martinez’s death, and the national organization later closed the NAU chapter.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy lawyer pushes back on claims he shifted strategy after mistrial in new interview
articles.summary: Kevin Reddington argued a Rule 25 motion claiming prosecutors failed to prove Lindsay Clancy killed her three children beyond a reasonable doubt.
articles.body: PLYMOUTH, Mass. — Lindsay Clancy's defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, is pushing back on claims that he changed strategies in court Tuesday when he raised doubts over whether prosecutors proved his client killed her three children, insisting he has attacked the strength of the Commonwealth’s case from the beginning. Reddington, speaking with Fox News contributor Billy Bush on his "Hot Mics" podcast, called the investigation into his client "horrific" and "atrocious" after arguing in court that prosecutors hadn't presented enough evidence in their case to prove his client guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. "That’s exactly what I was saying," Reddington said in the interview — right after Clancy's return to court for the first time since her mistrial. "I’ve been arguing that from the very beginning. I argued it in a closing argument to the jury. I argued in our motions." LINDSAY CLANCY LAWYER RAISES EXPLOSIVE DOUBT OVER WHO KILLED HER CHILDREN Reddington was arguing a Rule 25 motion for a required finding of not guilty, in which he is seeking to convince the court that the evidence given at trial wasn’t good enough to support a conviction. "Where’s the evidence that she did this?" Reddington asked Judge William Sullivan in court Tuesday, before running down a list of what he painted as insufficient evidence and faulty statements. "Where is the evidence she did this?" LINDSAY CLANCY'S LAWYER REVEALS POST-MISTRIAL STRATEGY AS RETRIAL LOOMS Although Reddington's comments on his motion for a required finding of not guilty garnered national headlines, Sullivan made no rulings and pushed oral arguments on other pending motions back to Nov. 2, leaving many who are following the case, including Bush, disappointed with the lack of answers. WATCH: Kevin Reddington describes Lindsay Clancy's demeanor as she fights murder charges "He didn't get any answers on the insufficiency of evidence," Bush told Fox News Digital Wednesday. "He wanted, immediately, her to be declared not criminally responsible because of that. I think that was a stretch. He probably knew it. He brought in his double jeopardy expert, Martin Weinberg. That was punted to Nov. 2. That wasn't immediately successful. And the alleged juror misconduct, we didn't get anything on that because Judge Sullivan, Reddington told us, impounded that information. We want to see the jury questionnaire. Everybody wants to see it." LINDSAY CLANCY JUDGE INDEFINITELY IMPOUNDS JUROR NAMES, CITING SAFETY AND 'DIVISIVE' ATTENTION Sullivan declared a mistrial on Sept. 4 after jurors could not agree on a verdict following roughly a week of deliberations. Rule 25 motions are routine but seldom successful, according to Carol Erskine, a retired Massachusetts judge and child welfare advocate who has been following the case closely. "I understand why people don’t get this, but he had to argue sufficiency of evidence under Rule 25(b)(2) case law. He told the judge he asked for a Bowden instruction and was denied, which meant he was challenging the poor investigation/search at the home by police. It’s a very nuanced argument." articles.title: Texas BBQ joint takes drastic step as soaring beef prices devour restaurant
articles.summary: Butter's BBQ near Corpus Christi in Texas dropped brisket from its menu after beef prices surged, with the beef cut eating over 70% of grocery costs.
articles.body: A Texas barbecue restaurant in the small town of Sinton, about a 30-minute drive from Corpus Christi, recently made the decision to remove brisket from its standard menu. The choice wasn't made overnight, Andrew Soto, the owner and operator of Butter's BBQ, told Fox News Digital. "We've been dealing with the price hikes, specifically in beef and briskets, for the better part of, I would say, five years," Soto said. AMERICA'S BEEF SUPPLY SHRINKS AS CATTLE FARMER WARNS 'THE NUMBERS ARE JUST NOT HERE ANYMORE' Soto noted that prices have fluctuated over the last five years, and, at times, they even appeared to be heading in the right direction. But over the last eight months to a year, beef prices climbed rapidly, and it eventually became too much to keep up with, he said. When the restaurant tried adjusting prices and cooking less brisket, its foot traffic and sales took a hit. CHICKEN WING PRICES ARE DOWN — HERE'S WHY YOUR FAVORITE RESTAURANT MAY NOT CUT PRICES "I guess the straw that broke the camel's back was last week. I was talking to one of my food reps, and he informed me that brisket had once again gone up in price," Soto said, noting that the price had increased by almost $1 per pound. That might not sound like a lot, he acknowledged, but it adds up when buying hundreds of pounds of beef at once. And in a small town, it's hard to anticipate how much people will buy. According to the USDA's Economic Research Service, beef and veal prices were 5.9% higher in August 2026 than in August 2025. In total, prices are expected to increase 9.4% in 2026, with a forecast interval of 7.4% to 11.6%. Fox News Digital reached out to the National Cattlemen's Beef Association for comment. It became too much of a "gamble," Soto said, to pay the steep prices for brisket and not be sure if the quantity he purchased would sell. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "It was a hard one, but I made the decision to pull our brisket from the menu completely," Soto said. The restaurant is currently experimenting with alternatives like beef cheek as a brisket alternative, but overall, pork is the priority, and Butter's BBQ is trying to encourage guests to reach for ribs and sausage. Soto clarified that the restaurant would still sell brisket, but not in the way or quantity it had been. "We're going to implement an online pre-order system where you'll be able to order it in advance, pay for it in advance," he said. Guests who really want brisket can still get their fix from Butter's, but it will not be part of the everyday menu. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "We're in Texas. It's a big deal," Soto said about brisket's popularity in the Lone Star State. A Facebook post in which Butter's BBQ shared the news about the menu change to its community said: "We apologize tremendously, we've done all we can to combat the constant price hikes, but we can no longer sustain our current business model with brisket eating up over 70% of our total grocery costs." "We're just trying to protect our business and our livelihood." Some people were shocked, commenting that brisket was an essential at any Texas barbecue joint. "In my opinion, not selling brisket will hurt your business," one Facebook commenter wrote. "Best move is to raise your prices to match the rising cost of beef. If your brisket is good then people will pay whatever price you set." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Another agreed, saying: "Just raise your prices, I've seen brisket sandwiches go from $10 to $12 up to $20." Other commenters were more understanding, with one commenter saying: "Bring on the pork!!!" Another offered a suggestion: "I'd love to see some smoked pork steaks. That could be an affordable alternative to add to the menu." Soto wants people to remember that the decision was not personal. "We're just trying to protect our business and our livelihood," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Please come and support us. We still have some really good barbecue, despite not having the brisket on our menu."

articles.title: These were the ‘Adams and Eves’ of facial recognition technology
articles.summary: For nearly a decade, the artist Trevor Paglen has exhibited the original faces that the U.S. military used to develop facial recognition technology. Now, we’ve all become the dataset.
articles.body: When we unlock our phones, pass through airport security, and — depending on where you live in the world — walk down the street, our faces are analyzed for the exact combination of nose width, eye spacing and jaw shape that allows an algorithm to see and recognize us. For billions of people, facial recognition technology has become part of daily life, allowing machines to assess our humanity and our physical identities in less than a second. In return for giving up this part of ourselves, we get a product or service or a sense of safety. But to learn all of our faces, it began with an original group. These “Adams and Eves” of facial recognition were part of a US Department of Defense initiative in the 1990s. Close to a decade ago, the artist Trevor Paglen was researching government datasets — which, though not widely seen, are in the public domain — when he came across one featuring the faces of thousands of government employees that the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency used to develop and train the nascent technology. Since then, he has exhibited a selection of the images as a series called “It Began as a Military Experiment,” which will display again in a 20-year retrospective of his work, “The Most Merciful Thing in the World,” that is also part of the FotoFocus Biennial in Cincinnati this month. Titled after an H.P. Lovecraft quote, the wider collection of his work examines what is often unseen or hidden from us, including photographs of hundreds of unidentified objects in Earth’s orbit, and hazy images of military sites magnified beyond what the human eye can see. Over the course of Paglen’s career, the themes he has explored across our relationship to technology, the ways in which we are surveilled, and the invisible technological processes that shape our world have only become more urgent. As an artist, Paglen explained by phone, “I honestly go back to the oldest trick in the book, which is take something familiar and make it strange, or take something strange and make it familiar.” He added: “But that what that means always changes because history is changing.” In “It Began as a Military Experiment,” the photographs show subjects of different ages, gender and skin tone against a blank sky-blue backdrop. Paglen ran each of the images through an algorithm to identify the points on the face that are measured and analyzed through facial recognition programs, and he shows the markers to the viewer — small white letters hovering over the corners of eyes and cupid’s bows and nostril edges, which translate people into data. The overall effect is uncanny. There is no way to place the subjects in time or space, beyond the occasional dated haircut. They mostly gaze off to the side, ignoring the camera. To the modern eye, a series of uniform, close-cropped portraits of a range of people might bring to mind the AI-generated portraits that at first shocked us with their realism. Now, we have to question every image put in front of us, looking for the increasingly more subtle signs that it might not be real at all. And, as AI has exploded, we have all quickly — and uncomfortably — had to adjust to the idea that we all have become the dataset on which these algorithms are trained, as they continue to gobble up our images and cultural output in the name of self-improvement. When I spoke to Paglen, it was the day after the Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon publicly announced on X that he had resigned from his job, and warned that the top labs building AI “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” In the weeks since, the mainstream discourse around AI has sharply turned for the worst. But it’s exactly the type of thing that Paglen has tried to capture in his work — the truest definition of the sublime, that heady mix of awe, beauty and horror in a world that’s beyond our cognitive understanding. “Our whole relationship to technology to me feels very supernatural, feels very in this world of cosmic horror,” he said. “And that is what our politics feels like to me as well. This YOLO, let’s-summon-every-demon-we can-imagine-and-see-what-happens feeling.” But when he created “It Began as a Military Experiment,” the conversations around the algorithms we were creating and the datasets we were feeding them were much different. In the mid-to-late 2010s, the conversations were largely around bias. Were algorithms used in policework prone to profiling? Was too much of our technology based on the perspective of privileged men? While those were all important conversations to have, he also believes it’s a fallacy to believe it could be designed differently. Ultimately, he said, they are tools of capitalism, tools for extraction, which will never care about being fair. “The bias conversation puts you in a position where it’s almost like you think it can be fixed and it is possible to have equitable AI systems, and that always felt wrong to me because once you introduce these things into a market logic, they are going to discriminate,” he explained. “That’s what they do, and you’re going to discriminate in order to figure out how to extract capital from different people in different ways.” Now when he looks back at these early facial recognition portraits, he feels their vulnerability more than anything else. The subjects were being photographed solely because they were government employees, and he wonders just how much they understood about the technology at the time and its implications. “If you’re being told to do this as part of your job, do you really consent?” he posed. “That’s one layer.” The other is that they couldn’t have possibly foreseen how our biometric data would underpin so many of our invisible systems today. “Is it possible to consent to have something that you did today used in the distant future in ways that you could not imagine?” he asked. “We retroactively become a part of systems that didn’t exist.” Yesterday it was them, today it’s all of us.

articles.title: Hegseth announces a new drone command and cuts to 20% of generals
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced some major changes to the U.S. military in what he called his “State of the Force” address, including establishing a new drone command and cutting 20% of the nation’s generals and admirals.
articles.body: QUANTICO, Va. — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced some major changes to the U.S. military on Wednesday in what he called his “State of the Force” address, including establishing a new drone command and cutting 20% of the nation’s generals and admirals. The Pentagon also will launch an effort to study the future of warfare that will be led in part by SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and former Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich, Hegseth said. The Defense Department will create an Office of Religious Affairs and plans to build a new base for the first time in 40 years, he added. Hegseth made the announcements to junior officers and enlisted leaders at the Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia — the second year in a row that he has given such an address. But this time, the U.S. military is seven months into a war with Iran with no clear end in sight, has captured Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and killed more than 200 people in strikes on alleged drug trafficking boats in Latin America, among other actions worldwide. The speech is not a usual fixture among Pentagon leaders. While Hegseth’s predecessors have regularly addressed troops and top officers, they have traditionally done so in small or private settings. The Pentagon chief, however, again led with how he has drastically retooled the U.S. military by targeting what he calls “woke” culture — through a rollback of diversity programs, a review of ground combat units with female troops and a new screening program for “testosterone deficiency” among male personnel — as well as attacks on the media for the coverage of the military. Hegseth announces a new drone-focused warfare command The Pentagon chief announced the intention to create a new four-star command to oversee the rollout of autonomous and robotic capabilities in what he called “the fastest peacetime shift in modern military history.” He acknowledged that “the pace of war is changing faster than the process to support it.” Iran commonly uses cheap drones, including those that have killed U.S. troops during the seven-month war. Hegseth pointed to Ukraine’s pioneering use of drones to combat Russian forces — something American forces have learned from firsthand. “Ukraine’s lesson is not that one type of drone wins wars, but rather the need for a purpose-built system that maximizes the ability to adapt,” Hegseth said. However, a U.S. Army unit based in Europe that specialized in drone warfare was ordered recently to end its efforts and return to being a traditional infantry battalion. A bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers subsequently asked the Army to explain the order, given that the world’s battlefields are rapidly evolving and military tactics increasingly rely on uncrewed systems to fight. The plans for a drone command come as the U.S. is in a stalemate with Iran over control of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy shipping corridor. The war has forced American forces in the region to expend hundreds of expensive missile interceptors to defend against Iran’s missile and drone attacks, which have still managed to kill and wound U.S. troops. Hegseth repeated claims that the U.S. military has destroyed Iran’s navy, air force and defense systems as well as many of its leaders and its industrial base. But Tehran has continued intermittently to launch drone and missile attacks against at U.S. or allied bases, while maintaining its ability to strike commercial and military ships in the Strait of Hormuz. During his speech, Hegseth touted the Trump administration’s major investments in the defense industry and push for contractors to speed up their work to expand the nation’s weapons arsenals. But experts say U.S. military contractors will need at least three years to replenish stockpiles of key weapons systems used heavily in the Iran war. Hegseth faces questions from lawmakers over cuts to general ranks. Hegseth said he directed the military services to double the 10% reduction he ordered last spring for roughly 800 flag and general officer positions, to a 20% decrease to be completed by Jan. 1, 2027. “I call it accountability and long overdue,” he said. Some members of Congress have criticized the war and the drawdown of munitions stockpiles, while calling the latest cuts to the general ranks a “purge” that will take years to rebuild. “He’s got some kind of like deep-seated grievance about leadership in the military,” said Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a former Navy combat pilot who has been critical of Hegseth. “He’s purging a generation of great leaders of the military, and it’s going to take a generation to recover from it.” Republican Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said he wanted to understand Hegseth’s reasoning. “If it’s simply a matter of eliminating a very heavy top, there may be some validity to it, but I want to see it first,” Rounds said. Musk and Gingrich to lead a study of future warfare In innovating the next wave of weapons systems, Hegseth announced an effort to study the future of warfare led by Musk, Gingrich and Palmer Luckey, co-founder of Anduril Industries. Hegseth said the work “will be focused on discovering, developing and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes.” He pointed to the need to dominate “any future battlefield, from under the Earth to beyond the moon.” This month, the U.S. confirmed for the first time that it had deployed weapons in space, a remarkable revelation after previous warnings about countries such as Russia possibly weaponizing a global frontier long agreed in treaties to be used for only peaceful purposes. Among the other announcements was the unveiling of a plan to build a new military base, with Hegseth inviting all 50 states to compete for the chance to play host to 15,000 to 25,000 service members. He also announced a plan to make every military base self-powered.

articles.title: Addis Ababa explosions: Blasts heard in Ethiopia's capital after drone flights banned
articles.summary: It comes a week after fighting erupted north of the capital between the army and a new alliance of armed groups.
articles.body:
Explosions were heard overnight in Ethiopia's capital, some in the area of the military headquarters in the west and another in the south of the city, residents and diplomatic sources say.

The blasts came hours after drone flights were banned over Addis Ababa and a week after fighting erupted in the north between the army and a newly launched alliance of armed groups including forces from the Tigray region.

A source linked to the opposition fighters told the Reuters news agency they were behind what they said were drone strikes.

"It was very loud. It was strong enough to set off car alarms," a resident in a southern area of the city, near the base of the secret service, told BBC Amharic.

He estimated that he heard the explosion in the Gotera neighbourhood some time around 00:30 local time (21:30 GMT).

Another resident told the BBC that he and his friends were playing games when they heard an explosion.

He lives in the western suburb of Torhayloch, a neighbourhood close to the military headquarters.

There were no official reports confirming the cause of the explosions, the exact locations affected or whether there were any casualties or damage.

The office of Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, the defence ministry as well as the federal and Addis Ababa police have not responded to BBC requests for comment.

Meanwhile, in a BBC interview, Eritrea's government has denied allegations made by Addis Ababa that it is backing the new rebel alliance.

Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray?

WATCH: Why are Ethiopia's rebels joining forces?

Clashes broke out last week after months of tension between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).

They both accuse each other of violating a 2022 peace deal that ended a brutal two-year civil war, which according to an Africa Union mediator is estimated to have cost 600,000 lives.

Last month, seven armed movements, including the TPLF and an Amhara militia known as Fano, formed an alliance with the stated aim of removing the government in Addis Ababa.

There is disagreement over which side started the latest fighting.

The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in the region.

The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas.

It is difficult to verify what is happening on the ground and access to the internet and the main telecoms service provider in Tigray have also been cut.

Within Tigray, the national army and a pro-government militia appear to be advancing towards the region's main city of Mekelle.

The TPLF is also reported to be fighting in neighbouring Afar region, a strategic area which connects landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti and its ports.

A humanitarian source has estimated that tens of thousands have fled their homes in Afar, according to the AFP news agency.

Fighting around Lalibela in the Amhara region, a Unesco world heritage site where foreign tourists have been stranded for more than a week, has involved the national army and Fano fighters, now allied to the TPLF.

The government has accused neighbouring Eritrea of backing these groups.

One pro-government militia commander fighting in Tigray told the BBC that Eritrean soldiers were involved on the front lines.

But in a rare response to the BBC from Eritrea's government, Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel dismissed the allegations.

He accused Ethiopia's ruling Prosperity Party (PP) of seeking external scapegoats for the country's mounting challenges.

"The PP regime has made it a habit to apportion blame to its neighbours in order to deflect attention from the myriad internal conflicts that it is fomenting in various parts of the country," he told BBC Tigrinya.

Eritrea was a key ally of Ethiopia during the Tigray war, fighting against the TPLF.

But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports.

Ethiopia lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993.

Abiy has even hinted at taking the port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - by force as he sees direct access to the sea as important for Ethiopia's long-term future and economic prosperity.

As concerns over security mount in Ethiopia, the country's National Intelligence and Security Service (Niss) announced on Wednesday that it was imposing an indefinite ban on drone flights in Addis Ababa and surrounding areas.

The agency said it would not issue permits for drone operations and warned that legal action would be taken against anyone flying drones in restricted areas.

Niss said the measure was necessary to protect national leaders, critical infrastructure and major public events.

articles.body: Carlos Ramon Obregon was 14 when he was killed in Los Angeles in 1977, but his identity resurfaced more than two decades later in a fraud case spanning 25 years. According to the US Department of Justice, an unidentified man used Obregon’s personal details to obtain identification documents and government benefits worth about $284,000. The man was convicted by a federal jury in May 2026 and sentenced in August to 61 months in prison. His real identity, however, remains unknown.How was the dead boy’s identity used for 25 yearsCourt records and evidence presented at trial showed that the identity theft began in 2000, 23 years after Obregon’s death. The defendant applied for a replacement Social Security card using Obregon’s Social Security number, date of birth and the names of his parents, according to the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Idaho.Obregon was born in Los Angeles in 1963. He was killed there in 1977 after suffering a gunshot wound to the head during a drive-by shooting, the Justice Department reported. He was buried at a local cemetery that same year.The case became particularly striking because the person using Obregon’s identity was never identified by authorities. During the May 2026 trial, Obregon’s mother testified that her son had died in 1977 and that the defendant was not her son.The stolen identity opened the door to government benefitsThe defendant went beyond obtaining a replacement Social Security card. Between 2004 and 2025, he fraudulently received about $177,000 in Supplemental Security Income, or SSI, under Obregon’s identity, according to the Justice Department’s May 2026 conviction announcement. He also obtained approximately $91,000 in Medicaid benefits between 2005 and 2025.A further $12,000 in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits was obtained between 2009 and 2025. During 2020 and 2021, the defendant also received about $3,200 in Economic Impact Payments issued during the COVID-19 pandemic.Together, those payments amounted to approximately $283,000 according to the May Justice Department release. At sentencing, the government placed the total at $283,977.40 and the court ordered that amount to be repaid as restitution.What identification documents did the man obtainThe stolen identity was also used to create a much wider set of official records. According to the Justice Department, the defendant obtained Idaho identification cards in 2002, 2010 and 2014. In 2022, he obtained an Idaho Star Card, again presenting Obregon’s birth certificate as evidence of his identity and lawful presence in the United States.The identity was also used to obtain a US passport. In 2012, the defendant applied for and received a passport using Obregon’s birth certificate. He subsequently travelled to Mexico several times using the document, according to the Justice Department.That passport eventually became a point of difficulty. In 2024, the defendant attempted to renew it, but the renewal was unsuccessful.The fraud was eventually brought to courtA federal jury in Pocatello heard the case during a 3-day trial in May 2026. On May 21, the jury found the defendant guilty of wire fraud, theft of government funds, aggravated identity theft and related charges, according to the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Idaho.The investigation involved several government agencies. The Justice Department credited the Social Security Administration Office of Inspector General, the State Department’s Diplomatic Security Service, the Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General, the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration, the Department of Agriculture Office of Inspector General and the Idaho Transportation Department.Their involvement reflected how the identity had been used across different government systems, from benefit programmes to state identification and international travel documents.However, the central mystery was not resolved by the trial. The man was convicted, but his actual identity remained unknown. The Justice Department said he appears in the case as a person whose identity has not been established.What sentence did the unknown man receiveOn August 25, 2026, US District Judge David C. Nye sentenced the defendant to 61 months in federal prison, equivalent to just over five years. The court also ordered 3 years of supervised release after his prison term and required him to pay $283,977.40 in restitution, according to the Justice Department.The case leaves a striking detail unresolved. Carlos Ramon Obregon died as a 14-year-old in 1977, yet his identity remained active in government records decades later. articles.title: Jewish human rights barrister, 94, arrested for supporting Palestine Action
articles.summary: Margaret Owen OBE, a celebrated human rights lawyer and friend of Ed Miliband’s late mother, talks to Al Jazeera.
articles.body:
London, United Kingdom – Margaret Owen, a 94-year-old Jewish human rights barrister, has been trying to get arrested for months.

She has attended about a dozen protests wearing a sign reading “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action” in London and has had a placard with those words attached to a window at her home since the group was proscribed under the Terrorism Act in the UK in July 2025.

But unlike thousands of others who have been detained for showing support for Palestine Action, officers had not – until Sunday – hauled her into a police van.

“I’ve been trying to get arrested for quite some time,” she told Al Jazeera. “I’m rather proud and glad to have finally joined the club.”

In her pursuit, Owen had also written to the Metropolitan Police, sharing photos and confessing, but “they’ve never done anything about it”.

“I think they never wanted to arrest me because that would be quite a story for the media, this ancient veteran human rights lawyer, aged 94, you know, it’s too much of a story.”

In Liverpool, during a rally held outside the Labour conference , she was finally detained.

“I was the oldest there … Maybe they’d never heard of me, the police up in Liverpool,” said Owen, who in 2013 received an OBE for her contribution to advancing women’s human rights, especially widows’.

Merseyside Police said 82 people were arrested in the same protest “on suspicion of wearing/carrying an article supporting a proscribed organisation” and have since been released on bail.

The Metropolitan Police did not comment on Owen specifically, but told Al Jazeera that, in London, “officers may not have witnessed an offence being committed, or the circumstances may not have met the necessary legal threshold for an arrest at that time”.

Owen said she wanted to be detained because the involvement of legal professionals lends a growing civil disobedience campaign “some sort of authority”.

The rallies have been organised by Defend Our Juries, a UK-based activist group demanding the UK lifts the ban on Palestine Action.

Founded in 2020, Palestine Action’s stated objective has been to counter Israeli war crimes – and what it says is British complicity in them – by targeting weapons manufacturers and associated companies. Its main target is Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest arms company, which has several facilities in the UK.

Several people who participated in raids claimed by Palestine Action are in jail, some having been sentenced as “terrorists” .

Many of those who have been arrested for showing support are pensioners, overwhelmingly for holding signs with the same seven words as the ones on Owen’s placard.

Doctors, teachers, lawyers, vicars, magistrates (many of them retired), a former adviser to King Charles and a Massive Attack singer are also among the diverse group, as is Tim Crossland, a coleader of Defend Our Juries and former government lawyer.

“I believe in the right to peaceful protest,” Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband recently told LBC radio. “I don’t think it was anyone’s intent to have those people criminalised,” he added, referring to the elderly and Christian leaders who have been detained.

As with the sanctions he announced against illegal Israeli settlements , his comments marked a departure from his predecessors.

Before Labour’s change of guard, few lawmakers under then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer criticised Israel’s conduct or the ban on Palestine Action. Just 10 voted against it in the House of Commons, compared with 276 for.

Then-Home Secretary Yvette Cooper ignored warnings from campaign groups, the United Nations human rights chief and leading politicians and peers that the move misused counterterrorism legislation.

“On the specific issue of Palestine Action, there’s a case coming before the Supreme Court, and so I’ll let that case play out, because I think it’s important that that court process takes its course,” Miliband told LBC.

He was referring to another case expected this year; Palestine Action’s cofounder Huda Ammori has been given permission to challenge the ban at the UK’s highest court.

Miliband, who is Jewish, has credited his late mother’s influence when explaining the UK’s new policies sanctioning Israel as it continues a genocidal campaign in Gaza.

“I admire and love Ed Miliband,” said Owen, who has a personal connection to the foreign secretary. She was “great friends” with Marion Kozak, his mother, a Holocaust survivor whose funeral she attended in July.

Kozak had “always been for the Palestinian people; she recognised the terrible Nakba of 1948”, said Owen, adding Miliband’s mother was moved by the plight “before many of us”.

‘I began to see how authoritarian Israel was’

Owen was born in 1932 to a family that also shouldered a painful history.

Her two great aunts and other relatives were killed in the Holocaust, “murdered in the forests of Paneriai in 1941 outside Vilnius”.

Her father was a lawyer and her mother, a doctor.

They were “very good parents”, she said. “I’m sure my mother would have been protesting like mad as well.”

Having studied law at the University of Cambridge, she qualified as a barrister at a time when the education system and legal profession were “very anti-women”. There were just two women studying law in her year, she said.

She later travelled to Israel for nine months, but after just three, “I began to see how authoritarian it was.”

“I began to see that whole indoctrination .”

She also remembered “how discriminate it was to all sorts of people, particularly the Black Jews, they called them, coming from Northern Africa”.

Along with her brother, who travelled with her, “we were questioning the Balfour Declaration ”.

“[The experience] made me very, very critical of Israel even from 1956 onwards.”

Throughout her career, she has worked on legal cases across the world.

In late December, Owen will learn more about her own case, whether she will be charged over her show of solidarity for Palestine Action.

“I’m afraid I’m not the terrorist,” she said. “But Israel is a terrorist state, and we are complicit in supporting a terrorist state.”

articles.title: Trump’s greatest gift to Xi: Making China America’s peer
articles.summary: U.S. allies have the most to lose. Major powers have repeatedly sought stability through exclusive understandings while middle powers and smaller states absorbed the consequences.
articles.body:
China has long sought peer validation from the only country whose recognition would carry decisive strategic weight — the U.S.

President Trump has now handed Beijing that prize. By repeatedly framing his summits with Chinese President Xi Jinping as a U.S.-China “G2” or “group of two,” Trump is granting China recognition as America’s principal strategic peer.

In fact, by hosting Xi last week for a state visit while world leaders gathered at the United Nations, Trump effectively portrayed the U.S.-China relationship as the axis of a bipolar world — a depiction that risks alienating U.S. allies and partners, such as Japan, India, Australia, the Philippines, Vietnam, South Korea and NATO members.

The symbolism surrounding the latest Trump-Xi summit was hard to miss. In an unprecedented departure from American diplomatic practice, Trump personally traveled to Joint Base Andrews, Md., to greet the arriving Xi with a lavish ceremony , which included a red carpet lined by U.S. service members and a military flyover featuring two B-1 bombers.

The following morning, a 479-member military honor guard greeted the Chinese leader during a White House arrival ceremony, capped by a flyover of a B-2 Spirit bomber escorted by four F-22 Raptors. Besides a state dinner, the visit also included a Trump-escorted tour of the National Archives.

These ceremonial flourishes communicated a powerful message: The leaders of the world’s two preeminent powers were meeting as equals.

More revealing than the pomp and pageantry of the summits with Xi has been Trump’s own language. He has repeatedly described his meetings with Xi as the G2. Before last October’s summit in Busan, South Korea, he announced on Truth Social, “THE G2 WILL BE CONVENING SHORTLY!” Afterward, he celebrated “My G2 meeting with President Xi.” Secretary of War Pete Hegseth also echoed the summit encounter as a “historic ‘G2 meeting.’”

Trump revived the G2 terminology during his Beijing visit in May, as if to highlight the formal end of the unipolar age . While previous American presidents carefully avoided legitimizing China’s claim to peer status, Trump’s use of the G2 concept during press encounters projected that the U.S. was now treating China as its true peer.

Trump has also been displaying a strikingly deferential posture toward America’s principal geopolitical rival. In the run-up to Xi’s Washington visit, Trump dismissed or excused reports of China’s actions against the U.S., such as providing Iran satellite imagery to target American assets, while portraying the Chinese leader as a personal friend, claiming he had “never gotten along better” with Xi.

Beijing has long rejected American hegemony while simultaneously seeking equal treatment from Washington. Beijing’s preferred phrase has been a “new model of major power relations” — a formula that seeks mutual respect for each side’s core interests, including China’s communist system and its territorial claims, including on Taiwan and the South China Sea.

The objective was not to establish a formal G2 institution but to normalize the idea that no major global issue could be decided without China. Trump’s summit diplomacy has brought Beijing much closer to realizing that objective.

The latest summit may have achieved little in concrete terms, with no agreement on any of the contentious bilateral issues and the truce in the trade war extended only by two months.

But for Xi, the visit was a propaganda coup , conveying to the Chinese people and the wider world that, under his leadership, China has become America’s equal. The optics indeed reinforced Beijing’s narrative of Xi-led national rejuvenation. Trump’s summit diplomacy has also helped Beijing advance one of the key objectives of its broader strategic messaging: demonstrating to domestic and international audiences that the U.S. can no longer dictate terms unilaterally.

Trump’s courtship of Xi represents a remarkable evolution from Trump’s first term, when tariffs, sanctions and technological restrictions were presented as instruments for reshaping China’s behavior. Today, Washington’s objective is no longer to transform China but to manage strategic rivalry through direct leader-to-leader bargaining, even if it means accepting the world’s largest autocracy as a co-equal on the global stage.

China is still not America’s equal in terms of economic, diplomatic or military power. But peer competition has never required matching strengths. The defining characteristic is the capacity to resist coercion and independently shape international outcomes. When Beijing last year responded to American tariffs by restricting rare-earth exports , it not only showed that economic interdependence cuts both ways but also demonstrated its capacity to impose retaliatory costs on the U.S.

The problem is not engaging a powerful rival to help avert costly miscalculations, but the public elevation of China into a privileged bilateral condominium. The real losers are likely to be America’s own allies and partners, whose interests could be subordinated to Washington-Beijing bargains , forcing them to hedge against U.S. unreliability.

The prospect of a U.S.-China duopoly, in which Washington and Beijing negotiate the rules of global governance while everyone else adjusts to the outcome, is a strategic nightmare for U.S. friends in Asia in particular. They want a stable balance of power, not a Sino-centric Asia.

History offers ample reason for their anxiety . Major powers have repeatedly sought stability through exclusive understandings while middle powers and smaller states absorbed the consequences.

The White House’s accommodative approach will likely gain greater salience as Trump has indicated that he will meet Xi again in November and December — first at the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen, China, and then at the G20 summit in Miami.

China’s greatest diplomatic victory in recent years has been won not on the battlefield or through economic coercion, but in Washington, where Trump has validated Beijing’s claim to peer status. For Xi, no concession could have delivered a more valuable prize than America itself recognizing China as a co-leader of the international system.

Brahma Chellaney is the author of nine books, including the award-winning “Water: Asia’s New Battleground. “

articles.title: Google DeepMind watermarks AI-generated protein as company chief AI scientist Demis Hassabis flags Biosecurity as urgent AI-era challenge
articles.summary: In what can be called a major breakthrough for synthetic biology and AI-powered biosecurity, Google DeepMind, Google’s AI lab, has developed a new method
articles.body: In what can be called a major breakthrough for synthetic biology and AI-powered biosecurity, Google DeepMind, Google’s AI lab, has developed a new method to watermark AI-designed proteins, establishing a permanent proof of origin directly inside biological code. Published in the journal Nature, the proof-of-concept technology, which is named SynthID Bio, solves a long-standing technical challenge: embedding an non-noticeable, verifiable digital identifier into biological sequences and predicted molecular structures without degrading their physical real-world utility in laboratory tests.The rollout comes amid rapid advancements in biological machine learning, where systems like AlphaFold 3, AlphaProteo and ProteinMPNN allow scientists to predict complex folding patterns and engineer functional binders. Yet these generative capabilities have heightened global biosecurity risks. Unfamiliar, machine-generated sequences can slip past conventional gene-synthesis filters, while unverified synthetic structural data risks contaminating open-access scientific repositories.‘An urgent challenge for the AI era’Google DeepMind Chief AI Scientist Demis Hassabis emphasised that guarding against biological misuse must be treated as a frontline safety priority for frontier AI:“Biosecurity is one of the most urgent challenges for the AI era. Bringing SynthID to biology so AI-generated proteins can be watermarked is a critical step - and we’re open sourcing SynthID Bio tools so the research community can build on this work. Published in @Nature today, congrats to the team!”Pushmeet Kohli, Vice President of Science at Google DeepMind and Chief Scientist at Google Cloud, celebrated the practical synthesis of these molecules:“Very happy to announce that our team at Google DeepMind has pushed the boundaries of generative biology, achieving the successful synthesis of AI-designed proteins that are both functional and watermarked. This proof-of-concept watermarking of the building blocks of life is enabled by SynthID Bio, our new protein watermarking method. It is designed to safeguard the new era of AI-powered generative biology and strengthen global biosecurity.”How SynthID Bio operatesSynthID Bio functions as a modular toolkit tailored across two primary dimensions of structural biology:SynthIDBio-sequence that subtly steers the selection of amino acid building blocks during sequence generation. In laboratory validation, watermarked protein binders engineered via AlphaProteo and a customized version of ProteinMPNN exhibited binding affinities on par with unmarked variants, while maintaining near-perfect watermark identification rates.SynthIDBio-structure relies on a fine-tuned iteration of AlphaFold 3 to insert an imperceptible mathematical watermark across atomic coordinate arrays, leaving a dependable detection signal without warping the molecular conformation.The signature persists beyond the digital blueprint: it remains fully detectable on the physical, synthesized protein itself after wet-lab manufacturing.You use AI every day. articles.title: Netanyahu: Copilot tried to crash plane after cockpit stabbing
articles.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Wednesday the Omani copilot who allegedly stabbed his captain on a flight to Israel was trying to crash the plane. During an appearance on CNN’s “The Brief,” Netanyahu praised the Indian pilot for displaying “incredible heroism” as he “somehow managed to unlock the door” to the cockpit after being…
articles.body:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Wednesday the Omani copilot who allegedly stabbed his captain on a flight to Israel was trying to crash the plane.

During an appearance on CNN’s “The Brief,” Netanyahu praised the Indian pilot for displaying “incredible heroism” as he “somehow managed to unlock the door” to the cockpit after being stabbed.

An Israeli passenger then “burst in,” threw the copilot back and took control of the aircraft, officials said, a FlyDubai plane en route from the United Arab Emirates (UAE) to Tel Aviv with 174 people on board.

“And then another Israeli, and I think another air crew member, they got control over the attacker, and then the reserve pilots who were in the passenger area came in, stabilized the airplane,” Netanyahu told host Jim Sciutto, adding the aircraft was dropping.

“So, the amazing heroism here of the Indian pilot, the Israeli passenger, and his colleagues, and those pilots managed to prevent a 9-11 disaster because that’s what it looks like was happening,” the Israeli prime minister added, referring to the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks on the U.S.

The plane eventually touched down safely at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia.

In a statement early Thursday, the UAE’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the country’s judicial authorities are investigating the incident.

The ministry added it will examine “any possible connection” to terrorist activity. Netanyahu noted Wednesday the copilot is being interrogated in Saudi Arabia and will be taken to the UAE “very soon.”

The Israeli leader added he spoke to UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who allowed Israel to “join” the interrogation.

“So, we’ll find out very soon if Iran had anything to do with it. But I can’t say that in advance of the conclusion of the interrogation,” Netanyahu told Sciutto.

articles.title: Christa Pike survives 2 lethal injections. How common are botched executions in the U.S.?
articles.summary: Christa Pike was hospitalized after surviving two doses of lethal injection drugs, prompting Tennessee to halt executions and investigate what went wrong.
articles.body:
Tennessee's only female death row inmate has been taken to the hospital after surviving two doses of lethal injection drugs, her lawyers said.

Christa Pike, 50, was alive and snoring loudly after being given two doses of pentobarbital, her attorneys said.

Pike had been scheduled for execution 10 a.m. Wednesday for a killing she committed in 1995, at the age of 18. She would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

An appeals court stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start, a stay that was subsequently overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court.

Media witnesses said officials raised the curtains to the execution chamber at 7:27 p.m., showing Pike strapped to a gurney. "I'm going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life, and that is in love," she said in her "last" words.

However, Pike remained conscious after the initial dose and at one point raised her head and asked prison officials if her arm was supposed to feel that way.

By 8:26 p.m., witnesses reported that the second dose of pentobarbital had been administered.

Pike continued to be heard snoring behind the closed curtain until the microphone was cut off at 8:53 p.m. At that time, an announcement was made to escort media witnesses out of the area.

Pike's legal team said in a statement to the Tennessean newspaper, "Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution.

"We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy."

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said that he had ordered "a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred" and that the remaining scheduled execution will not take place this year.

"Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the state's most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective," he said.

Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said what Pike experienced was "singular and unparalleled."

Seven other people have survived medical problems caused by an execution team's failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one has remained alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions, she said.

"I've witnessed, I believe, five executions in Tennessee," said Tori Gessner, a journalist with WKRN News 2 in Nashville. "Nothing about today was normal, typical at all, and the court delay was just the tip of the iceberg."

The Tennessee Department of Correction said that it "followed every step of the state's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general's office."

The state's execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered "if the inmate is not deceased" after the first set. It does not specify what happens if the subject is still alive after the second set.

Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion late Wednesday with the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in "unnecessary agony" and that the execution was violating her right to be free from cruel and unusual punishment. They also filed motions in the Sixth Circuit and a district court.

Pike was sentenced to death in 1996 after being convicted of first-degree murder of Colleen Slemmer the previous year on the University of Tennessee Agricultural campus. Pike was also convicted of attempted first-degree murder after trying to strangle fellow inmate Patricia Jones in 2001.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center (DPI), there have been 64 well-known botched execution attempts between 1982 and the first half of 2026 across the U.S. Most of these were executions that went wrong in some way, but still ended in death. It acknowledges that the number is an approximation. It has listed the individual cases on its website.

Of those 64, the DPI says seven execution attempts resulted in failure. It said the execution of Tennessee inmate Tony Carruthers — which failed when staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal drug — was the most recent it had documented before Pike.

The DPI, which says it does not take a position on the death penalty itself but is critical of problems in its application, cites figures showing that, historically, around 3 % of attempted executions between 1890 and 2010 were flawed. Lethal injection has drawn particular scrutiny, with 7.2% of attempted executions being botched, the DPI said, compared with the rate of 3.15% across all methods, including electrocution, hanging and gas.

Experts have pointed to difficulties establishing intravenous lines, questions about the drugs used and the ethical role doctors can play in executions , since their ethics code requires them to swear to preserve life.

Such figures on botched executions have been questioned by some, including Michael Conklin, an assistant professor of business law at Texas A&M University–Central Texas. In a 2020 paper , he argued that some of the cases classified as botched attempts included those in which the prisoner resisted, those in which there were difficulties inserting the IV, and those in which prison officials opened the curtain too early.

The state of Tennessee has experienced recent issues that predate Pike's case.

In April 2022, Gov. Lee called off the execution of Oscar Smith about an hour before it was scheduled to begin after the state discovered that its lethal injection drugs had not been properly tested. An independent investigation found that the state had repeatedly failed to follow its own drug-testing protocols between 2018 and 2022.

Tennessee then revised its protocol, resuming executions in May 2025 and using a single, lethal drug, pentobarbital.

Pike's failed execution was Tennessee's second this year . Carruthers, who was convicted of the kidnapping and murders of three people in Memphis, was scheduled to be executed on May 21, 2026, but officials abandoned the attempt after they were unable to establish the intravenous access needed to administer the drug. The ACLU , which was part of his legal team, said witnesses reported more than an hour of attempts to establish a line while Carruthers groaned in pain.

Families of victims, however, may feel differently. The family of Slemmer, Pike's victim, traveled to Nashville expecting to witness the execution. Her mother, May Martinez, told the Associated Press she had waited decades to see it happen, "Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run," she said.

There were 47 executions in 2025 , according to the DPI, higher than the recent average of fewer than 30 per year. These included the lethal injection of South Carolina inmate Marion Bowman , who received twice the intended drug dose, and Tennessee inmate Byron Black , who reportedly showed sustained cardiac activity for nearly two minutes after prison staff pronounced him dead.
